questions.prompt: Order the phases of one TDD cycle.

items.text: Red — write a small failing test
Green — write the simplest code to pass it
Refactor — clean up while tests stay green

questions.explanation: TDD runs red (failing test), green (simplest passing code), refactor (improve design), then repeats.

questions.prompt: Why is watching the test fail first important?

options.text: It makes the suite run faster
A failing test proves it actually checks the new behavior
pytest requires at least one failure

questions.explanation: If a test passes before the code exists, you can't trust it to catch anything; the red step proves the test has teeth.

options.text: Adding a second example that a hard-coded answer can't satisfy, forcing real logic

questions.explanation: Triangulation adds another case so a constant 'fake it' answer no longer passes, driving out the general implementation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about TDD are honest and accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: TDD gives a regression net that makes refactoring safer
TDD does not replace integration, E2E, or edge-case testing
Every behavior ends up with a test that once failed

questions.explanation: TDD provides a safety net and meaningful tests but does not guarantee good design or replace other test levels.

questions.prompt: The technique of returning a hard-coded value just to reach green, then generalizing, is called '____ it till you make it'.
questions.explanation: 'Fake it till you make it' gets you to green quickly; later tests (triangulation) force the real implementation.

questions.prompt: Match each TDD phase or idea to its purpose.

pairs.right: Write a failing test for the next behavior
Make it pass as simply as possible
Improve the design while tests stay green
Localize mistakes and keep feedback fast

questions.explanation: The cycle plus small steps is what makes TDD a tight feedback loop.
